title: #stitch with @Kate Reinking - Also, I obviously also haven’t seen eve...
transcript: she even gave them a backstory for coming to Neverland just like the Lost Boys have a backstory for being there this is fascinating to me because I've always thought that the reason so many Peter Pan adaptations try and fail to address the problem with Tiger Lily and the indigenous characters is because their presence in Neverland is what's inherently racist like a lot of adaptations will just tone down the stereotypes try to present them in a way that's a little more dignified maybe even make them more important to the story but then it doesn't really work because it's like okay, but they're still in *Neverland* like correct me if I'm wrong but my understanding has always been that the reason there are indigenous characters in Peter Pan in the first place is that JM Barrie was essentially using them as like set dressing or as like symbol for childhood fantasy playtime adventure same as the Pirates which is obviously very reductive and dehumanizing to this real life culture (or group of cultures as it is in real life although you wouldn't know it from Peter Pan) which is why no matter how respectfully you try to present them it doesn't really work because it's the literal location of the story that is framing them in a problematic way but until now, I'd never heard of an adaptation that actually tried to establish a different reason for why they're there in the first place that's really interesting to me Who ever could have guessed that it would be an indigenous writer who would come up with a solution to this problem? crazy right?! I should clarify that I haven't actually seen this production for myself I would like to, but I haven't had the opportunity so I don't actually know how it works in context but on paper at least from the way Kate describes it seems like a clever workaround for the problem. maybe it does raise other questions like Kate said later in their video like if the indigenous characters have a backstory for arriving in Neverland why don't the pirates, if they were kind of there for the same reason? so yeah I could definitely see how like maybe you could see the seams in it a little bit but it’s probably the best we could expect for this specific musical but I don't know, I'd be curious to hear other people's thoughts on this especially if you've seen the production and of course especially if you are indigenous yourself I'm not, I'm just a guy who's seen a lot of Peter Pan adaptations and thought a lot about this
classificationReason: Stitch/reply video responding to someone else's content about Peter Pan adaptations and indigenous representation. Creator states they haven't seen the shows being discussed.
